Question: For the game show Who Wants To Be a Millionaire? the dollar values of each question are shown in the following table (where \(\text{K}=1000\)). \[ \begin{array}{ccccc} \boldsymbol{\#} & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \boldsymbol{\$} & 100 & 200 & 300 \end{array} \]\[ \begin{array}{cccccc} 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ 500 & 1\text{K} & 2\text{K} & 4\text{K} & 8\text{K} \end{array} \] \[ \begin{array}{ccccc} 9 & 10 & 11 & 12 \\ 16\text{K} & 32\text{K} & 64\text{K} & 125\text{K} \end{array} \] \[ \begin{array}{ccc} 13 & 14 & 15 \\ 250\text{K} & 500\text{K} & 1000\text{K} \end{array} \] Between which two questions is the percent increase of the value the smallest?
Solution:
A percent increase compares the gain with the original value, so use
\[
\frac{\text{new value}-\text{original value}}{\text{original value}}\times100\%.
\]
Every adjacent step in the table doubles the value except the steps from \(2\) to \(3\), from \(3\) to \(4\), and from \(11\) to \(12\). Doubling is a \(100\%\) increase. For the three exceptions, the increases are
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\text{ to }3 &: \frac{300-200}{200}\times100\%=50\%,\\
3\text{ to }4 &: \frac{500-300}{300}\times100\%=66\tfrac23\%,\\
11\text{ to }12 &: \frac{125-64}{64}\times100\%=95.3125\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the last calculation, measuring both values in thousands leaves the ratio unchanged. The smallest increase is \(\boxed{50\%}\), from question \(2\) to question \(3\), choice \(\text{B}\).
